name: Things 3
subcategory: personal tasks, routines and daily planning
tagline: Build a polished personal task manager with areas, projects, tags, deadlines, and a today view

pricing.notes: Sold as separate one-time app purchases; canonical monthly price is null.

tiers.name: Things for Mac
tiers.limits: 1 Mac App Store license; 15-day direct-download trial.

pricing.billingTerms: one-time purchase per Apple platform; no subscription or annual plan
pricing.hiddenCosts: Mac, iPhone/Watch, iPad, and Vision are separate purchases; there is no cross-platform bundle, though Things Cloud sync is free.

verdictSummary: The core loop is small enough for a capable coding agent to produce a useful local version in one sitting. For Things 3, build a polished personal task manager with areas, projects, tags, deadlines, and a today view. The hard boundary is exceptional native design, apple-device sync, shortcuts, and long-term maintenance, plus cross-device reliability and workflow polish.
coreLoopDIY: Capture tasks into areas and projects with tags and deadlines, schedule or repeat them, work from a focused today view, and keep history locally.
whatYouLose: exceptional native design, Apple-device sync, shortcuts, and long-term maintenance
ongoingBurden: recurrence edge cases, notifications, sync conflicts, calendar APIs, mobile capture, and backups
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for Things 3 because task software is sticky because trust, speed, and ubiquitous capture matter more than the database schema. The recurring cost buys recurrence edge cases, notifications, sync conflicts, calendar APIs, mobile capture, and backups, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: Vikunja
priorArt.desc: Mature open-source task and project manager with lists, kanban, and recurring work.

alternatives.name: Apple Reminders
alternatives.desc: Things minus the polish tax, provided every device in sight has an Apple logo

facts.install: Preinstalled on iPhone, iPad, and Mac; enable iCloud or another supported reminders account for synchronization
facts.engines: Optional Apple Intelligence can suggest or auto-categorize reminders on supported devices; ordinary task management does not require AI
facts.dataFormat: Structured reminder records live in iCloud or another configured reminders account and are cached on Apple devices; iCloud provides account-level restore rather than user-visible task files
facts.gapVsPaid: Apple Reminders is less coherent and polished than Things for organizing Areas, multi-step projects, headings, start dates, deadlines, and the Today-to-Upcoming flow.

alternatives.name: Microsoft To Do
alternatives.desc: A polished free task manager, paid for with a Microsoft account rather than money

facts.install: Install the Windows, macOS, iOS, or Android app, or use the web app, and sign in with a Microsoft account
facts.dataFormat: Tasks are stored as structured records on Microsoft's Exchange Online servers and surface in Outlook Tasks across synchronized clients
facts.gapVsPaid: Microsoft To Do lacks Things’ refined Areas-and-project hierarchy, headings, start-versus-deadline distinction, and Apple-native interaction polish.

alternatives.name: Super Productivity
alternatives.desc: A local task manager with timeboxing, Pomodoro, and no account begging to be created

facts.install: Use the browser/PWA or install a packaged desktop or mobile build
facts.dataFormat: Tasks, projects, time records, and settings are local-first in browser or app storage; optional synchronization and backups use the user's chosen WebDAV or Dropbox account
facts.gapVsPaid: Super Productivity is busier and more time-tracking-oriented than Things and lacks its exceptionally polished native Apple quick-capture and planning flow.

alternatives.name: Vikunja
alternatives.desc: A capable Todoist replacement once you accept becoming its hosting department

facts.install: Use the paid hosted service or deploy the free server with Docker Compose, a package, or the standalone binary
facts.dataFormat: Tasks, projects, users, and settings live in SQLite, MySQL/MariaDB, or PostgreSQL, with attachments in a persistent files directory, on the selected host
facts.gapVsPaid: Vikunja feels like a hosted web task system and cannot match Things’ native offline polish, frictionless capture, or elegant Today and Upcoming experience.
facts.setupBlocker: The free path requires a server or Docker, persistent volumes, secrets, and normally a reverse proxy with TLS

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Mac license plan and a personal desktop task manager DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a personal replacement for Things 3 in an empty repository.
Use Tauri 2, React, TypeScript, SQLite, and desktop notifications; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: capture tasks into areas and projects with tags and deadlines, schedule or repeat them, work from a focused today view, and keep history locally.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Create inbox, today, upcoming, someday, and completed views with fast keyboard capture.
Support projects, tags, due dates, start dates, priorities, notes, subtasks, and attachments.
Implement robust daily, weekly, monthly, and custom recurring rules with tests.
Add a focus view with one active task, timer, and optional desktop notification.
Provide search, saved filters, undo, and a completed-task archive.
Export and import a documented JSON format and make automatic local backups.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Deliberately leave out team assignment and comments.
Deliberately leave out two-way calendar or email synchronization.
Deliberately leave out native mobile apps and cloud accounts.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
